items.headline: Disueño 2026 Adds New Delta Prize Category for Limited Editions
items.background: The Delta Prizes, run by ADI-FAD, are a long-running Spanish industrial design award. The new Disueño category revives a concept from exhibitions held fifty years ago, specifically targeting unique or limited-run design work.
keyFindings: A new award category called Disueño has been added to the 2026 Delta Prizes
The category is inspired by ADI-FAD's Disueño exhibitions from roughly the 1970s
It targets unique or limited-edition designed objects, distinguishing them from mass-produced work
items.implications: Relevant for designers working in limited-run, craft, or experimental product design who may want to submit work or track what the industry is recognizing as distinct from mainstream industrial design.

items.headline: Cognition Buys AI Personality Studio Poke for Nine Figures
items.background: Cognition, the company behind the AI coding agent Devin, has acquired Poke, a startup focused on AI personality and character design. The nine-figure price signals serious investment in making AI agents more human-feeling, not just more capable.
keyFindings: Cognition acquired Poke for a nine-figure sum — at minimum $100 million
The acquisition is framed as an 'AI personality play,' indicating focus on agent character and tone rather than raw capability
This follows a broader industry pattern of AI companies investing in anthropomorphization and user-facing personality layers
items.implications: For product and UX teams designing with or around AI agents, this signals that personality, tone, and character are becoming competitive differentiators — not just interface polish. Worth tracking how Cognition integrates Poke's work into Devin and similar tools.

items.headline: UX Research Output Is Becoming Context for AI, Not Humans
items.background: As AI tools take on more interface generation work, there's a growing question about what UX research and design documentation is actually for. This piece argues the audience for that output is shifting from human designers to AI systems that use it as generative context.
keyFindings: The author argues that as AI generates more interfaces, UX research output should be structured as AI-readable context rather than human-readable documents
This reframes the deliverable of a UX researcher from reports and decks to curated, structured prompts or context files
The shift has implications for how research is written, stored, and handed off within product teams
items.implications: Directly actionable for researchers and design leads: if AI tools are being used to generate interfaces on your team, evaluate whether your existing research formats — personas, journey maps, briefs — are structured in ways an AI system can actually use. This likely requires rethinking documentation conventions.

items.headline: Product Sense Is Pattern Recognition With Judgment About When Patterns Apply
items.background: 'Product sense' is frequently cited in hiring and performance discussions but rarely defined precisely. This piece offers a concrete, operational definition and a method for building it deliberately rather than treating it as innate intuition.
keyFindings: Product sense is defined as the ability to predict which product decisions will succeed, based on patterns learned through experimentation
A critical component is meta-cognitive: knowing when a given pattern applies to the current situation and when it does not
The definition implies product sense can be systematically developed through structured experimentation and reflection, not just accumulated experience
items.implications: Useful for anyone hiring for or developing product roles. The definition gives managers a concrete basis for evaluating product sense in interviews and for structuring growth plans — moving away from vague 'good instincts' language toward testable, observable behaviors.
